# Lesson evidence in one line each

152 lessons. This is the one file that lists every lesson (besides llms-full.txt, which holds everything). To choose lessons: scan this file, then open the aspect page (the heading link) only for the lessons you use; it holds the full "Against" line, the Era (years and newest model family) and the legend. Each line: ID, tag (stated by a source, or ours), the lesson, then oracle (does the evidence rely on the old system), model (does it depend on model ability), strength, "may be outdated" where it applies, the cases it cites, and the cases its "Against" line cites.

## [Planning and scoping](planning.md)

- **PLN-1** [stated] Pilot the whole pipeline (build, CI, review, packaging, release) on a few easy, well-tested units, and settle the conventions before fanning out to the rest. Oracle partly; model no; strong. Cases: Bun, GitHub, Google, Airbnb, Lutz Leonhardt. Against: Bun.
- **PLN-2** [stated] Expect most of the effort to go into specs, porting guides, manifests and tooling before the bulk run; schedule and staff that phase, not only execution. Oracle no; model no; strong. Cases: 1Password, Bun, GitHub, Uber. Against: Airbnb.
- **PLN-3** [stated] Re-measure scope while the work runs; in a live repository, code moving into scope and code written meanwhile can multiply the first estimate. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub. Against: none found; a limit from Airbnb.
- **PLN-4** [stated] Order the slices along the dependency graph, leaves first and the most connected hub last, and approach the hub from one direction only. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Intel, 1Password. Against: disagree: Christopher Chedeau.
- **PLN-5** [stated] Translate first and redesign later: keep behaviour the same during the move so that any failure points at the port, not at a deliberate change. Oracle yes; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun, Christopher Chedeau, Ping.gg, Ladybird, Mindstone, Checkly. Against: disagree: Intel, Shopify, Datadog, Robert Marshall.
- **PLN-6** [stated] Set expectations per class of work: bounded, repetitive edits gain a lot; work with ordering, schema or shared-state constraints gains far less. Oracle no; model yes; medium. Cases: 1Password, Spotify, Zalando, Temporal. Against: Uber.
- **PLN-7** [ours] Reopen rewrites shelved for cost, since agents change the price; but weigh them against doing nothing, not against a manual rewrite nobody would fund. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub, 1Password. Against: Slack, 1Password, Temporal.
- **PLN-8** [stated] Leave out segments you cannot specify or verify (non-standard repositories, unsupported platforms, languages the model handles poorly) instead of forcing one approach on all. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Spotify, Google, Uber, Bloomberg. Against: Bloomberg.
- **PLN-9** [ours] Plan for a partial outcome and a stop rule: abandoned attempts appear here only inside stories that end in a success, so success odds read from such cases are inflated. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Slack, 1Password, Spotify, Airbnb, Ping.gg, Robert Marshall. Against: Uber, Ping.gg.
- **PLN-10** [stated] Measure how often each pattern (runner, rule, base class) is used and how automatable it is, and build the transforms or prompts with the best return first. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Uber, Bloomberg. Against: none found; a limit from Bloomberg.
- **PLN-11** [stated] Do not port a whole app in one pass, even from specs gathered first; Shopify's author says that gives code nobody can maintain. Port in small ordered slices a person can review quickly. Oracle partly; model partly; weak. Cases: Shopify, Christopher Chedeau. Against: disagree: Bun, Ladybird, Christopher Chedeau.
- **PLN-12** [stated] Sort targets into archetypes, each with its own prompt, data collection and checks; give rare archetypes a generic starting point instead of dedicated automation. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Bloomberg, Mindstone. Against: Airbnb.
- **PLN-13** [stated] In a framework or data-store move, build the target's foundation (architecture, data model) in its own idiom first, then port old parts onto it; one straight port rebuilt the old layers. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Robert Marshall, Datadog. Against: none found; a limit from Datadog.

## [Testing and oracles](testing.md)

- **TST-1** [stated] Use a black-box suite that does not depend on the implementation language as the oracle, and run it unchanged against the old code and the new. Oracle yes; model no; strong. Cases: Bun, GitHub, Ping.gg, Ladybird, Datadog, Mindstone, Checkly. Against: Bun, Ladybird, Checkly, Mindstone, Datadog.
- **TST-2** [stated] Before the move starts, make sure tests cover the behaviour that matters and that agents can run them; the gaps were where missing-feature regressions came from. Oracle yes; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Spotify, Ping.gg, Lutz Leonhardt, Checkly. Against: Google, Intel.
- **TST-3** [stated] Equivalence with the old system is not correctness: a faithful port carries the old bugs, and tests can assert the wrong behaviour with confidence. Oracle yes; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub. Against: Bun.
- **TST-4** [ours] Run the oracle on the build configuration you ship; debug-only assertions and checks hid regressions that appeared only in release builds. Oracle partly; model no; weak. Cases: Bun. Against: none found.
- **TST-5** [stated] Where the old system has thin tests, record its inputs and outputs (or have a separate agent write equivalence tests) and replay them against the new code. Oracle yes; model partly; medium. Cases: Intel, Slack, Mindstone, Checkly. Against: Intel, Mindstone, Christopher Chedeau.
- **TST-6** [stated] Make the baseline green before agents start: fix tests that already fail and make golden files regenerable, or correct changes stall at the gate. Oracle yes; model no; medium. Cases: Google, Spotify. Against: Lutz Leonhardt.
- **TST-7** [ours] When a move touches numeric types or sums (a widened ID, a new engine's arithmetic), test values beyond the old range at real data sizes; small examples pass while overflow survives. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: Google, Temporal. Against: none found.
- **TST-8** [ours] When the migrated artefact is itself a test, passing is a weak oracle; also compare test counts, coverage and intent file by file. Oracle yes; model no; weak. Cases: Slack, Airbnb, Uber, Asana. Against: none found.
- **TST-9** [stated] Treat performance as part of the contract: benchmark end to end against a deterministic local stand-in for slow services, and count slowdowns as regressions. Oracle yes; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Ladybird. Against: no case linked, see page.
- **TST-10** [ours] Keep the agent that writes code apart from the one that writes its tests; one generation producing both invites checks that cannot fail. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Intel. Against: Intel.
- **TST-11** [stated] Test the prompts too: rerun a golden set of before-and-after examples after each prompt edit or model trial; small wording changes swung results. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Zalando. Against: none found.
- **TST-12** [stated] Check parity on what users and downstream systems see: capture screens, raw events or query answers from old and new at the same points, ignoring values that vary per run. Oracle yes; model no; medium. Cases: Shopify, Zalando, Datadog, Temporal. Against: none found; a limit from Shopify.
- **TST-13** [stated] Make the old code's output deterministic and dumpable before porting, then run old and new side by side on real inputs and stop at the first difference. Oracle yes; model no; weak. Cases: Ladybird. Against: Checkly, Mindstone, Ladybird.
- **TST-14** [stated] Never make coverage alone the target of agent-written tests: it rose while the tests asserted nothing. Fail any test that leaves a side effect or response field unasserted. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Mindstone. Against: none found; a limit from Mindstone.
- **TST-15** [stated] Model the harness's surrounding infrastructure on production down to each queue and table; the agent builds to what the tests show, so a simplified layout ships as a bug. Oracle partly; model partly; weak. Cases: Checkly. Against: none found.

## [Verification loops and gates](verification.md)

- **VER-1** [stated] A clean compile or a green CI run shows the parts fit together, not that behaviour survived; plan a behavioural check after it. Oracle partly; model no; strong. Cases: GitHub, Intel, Spotify, Zalando, Bloomberg, Christopher Chedeau, Lutz Leonhardt, PagerDuty. Against: Bun, Bloomberg.
- **VER-2** [stated] Order gates from cheap to costly and drop a candidate at its first failure, with cheap no-change checks (whitespace only, unchanged syntax tree) up front. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: Google, Uber. Against: Airbnb, Slack, Spotify.
- **VER-3** [stated] Retry a failed unit with its latest errors in a fresh prompt, cap the attempts, and hand what remains to people; this fits independent units, such as one file each. Oracle partly; model partly; strong. Cases: Airbnb, Google, Spotify, Bloomberg. Against: Google, Intel, Uber, Bun.
- **VER-4** [stated] Give the agent one verify tool that picks the right build and test runner and returns short errors, and run it automatically before the agent may finish. Oracle partly; model partly; weak. Cases: Spotify. Against: GitHub.
- **VER-5** [stated] Before trusting a green suite, confirm the tests really ran: compare executed tests and assertions with the baseline, and count skips as failures. Oracle yes; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, Slack, Lutz Leonhardt. Against: none found; a limit from Lutz Leonhardt.
- **VER-6** [stated] Check output against machine-readable contracts (generated signatures, schema-compatibility checks) so a dropped or changed interface fails mechanically. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: Intel, GitHub. Against: GitHub.
- **VER-7** [stated] Define done as an empty list of change sites produced by deterministic tooling and rerun on a schedule, never as the agent's own report. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: Google, 1Password, Christopher Chedeau, Lutz Leonhardt, GitLab. Against: Google, Christopher Chedeau.
- **VER-8** [stated] Rank failures by cost: no change is cheap, a red change costs an engineer, a green but wrong change costs trust; aim verification at the last kind. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Spotify, GitHub, Zalando, Bloomberg. Against: none found.
- **VER-9** [stated] Where the target has no tests the agent cannot check itself: leave it out, require tests first, or budget for owners to test each change. Oracle partly; model no; weak. Cases: Spotify. Against: Intel.
- **VER-10** [stated] Where one change repeats across many targets, keep the pass/fail gates deterministic as the model writes more; an error a model-run gate lets through can spread to every target. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Bloomberg. Against: disagree: Google, Spotify, Shopify, Bun.
- **VER-11** [stated] Before building the pipeline, judge how late a wrong change first fails; changes that only the owner's deploy could check were merged less and rejected more. Oracle partly; model no; weak. Cases: Bloomberg. Against: none found; a limit from Bloomberg.

## [Code review](review.md)

- **REV-1** [stated] Never let the writing agent review its own change; use two or more reviewers in fresh contexts that see only the diff and are told to find faults. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub, Ladybird, Mindstone. Against: Bun, GitLab.
- **REV-2** [stated] Split the review: agents and tests do the exhaustive old-against-new comparison; people spend their attention on architecture, contracts and flagged risk. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun. Against: disagree: Slack, Google, Shopify, Zalando, Ping.gg.
- **REV-3** [ours] Give reviewers a written list of constructs that read the same in old and new code but behave differently: assertions, eager defaults, falsy checks, number types, built-in validators, equality. Oracle yes; model partly; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub, Lutz Leonhardt, PagerDuty. Against: none found; a limit from Lutz Leonhardt.
- **REV-4** [stated] Add an automatic scope check that compares each diff with its instruction; agents drift into refactors, switched-off tests and side fixes. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Spotify, Google. Against: Spotify.
- **REV-5** [ours] Treat LLM reviewers and judges as unmeasured until you know their miss rate; veto counts and showcase catches say nothing about what got through. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: Spotify, Bun, Lutz Leonhardt, GitLab. Against: GitHub.
- **REV-6** [stated] Have the tool leave an inline note with a guide link at each spot it deliberately left for a person, so reviewers find the judgement calls fast. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Spotify, Slack. Against: none found.
- **REV-7** [stated] Let people see only changes that already built and passed tests; developers counted that filter as one of the largest gains. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: Google. Against: Google, Spotify.
- **REV-8** [stated] Audit the reviewers and the fixer: check that AI reviewers flag real differences and that the agent's answers to review comments hold up. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub. Against: none found.
- **REV-9** [stated] Once agents write fast, review, testing and deploy by the owning teams become the bottleneck; plan for that load from the start: reviewer capacity, evidence that eases review, priority. Oracle no; model partly; strong. Cases: GitHub, Google, Spotify, Bloomberg, GitLab. Against: Bloomberg, Asana.
- **REV-10** [ours] Grade a small sample of converted code against hand-converted versions with a rubric; pass rates say nothing about readability or idiom. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: Slack, Ladybird. Against: Airbnb.
- **REV-11** [stated] Code that meets the feature requirements can still duplicate logic, drift from the architecture or run slowly; keep reviewers who know the target platform. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Shopify, Christopher Chedeau, Datadog. Against: disagree: Christopher Chedeau.

## [Release and rollout](rollout.md)

- **ROL-1** [stated] Swap one component per change inside normal releases, old and new in one tree joined by a temporary bridge, so the main branch can always ship. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Uber, Ladybird. Against: disagree: Bun, Shopify, Mindstone.
- **ROL-2** [stated] Treat merged and released as separate gates: ship first to a canary or pre-release that few users take, and promote it only after real use. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub, Google, Checkly. Against: GitHub, GitLab.
- **ROL-3** [stated] Changes that reach many teams' systems still need slow production rollouts watched by their owners; the AI pipeline speeds the code, not this step. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Google, Bloomberg, GitLab. Against: Bun.
- **ROL-4** [stated] Delete the old code in the same change that adds the new; concurrent edits to ported code then surface as rebase conflicts instead of silent losses. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: GitHub. Against: GitHub.
- **ROL-5** [stated] Keep agent branches short-lived against a busy main branch; sessions left open for days pile up drift, and rebases lose changes. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: GitHub. Against: none found.
- **ROL-6** [ours] Track the size of the temporary bridge between old and new as the progress signal and drive it to zero; line counts on a busy code base mislead. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: GitHub. Against: none found.
- **ROL-7** [stated] Ship a new failure boundary (such as hosting in-process) as an opt-in mode beside the old default, separate from the code port itself. Oracle partly; model no; weak. Cases: GitHub. Against: none found.
- **ROL-8** [stated] When old and new run side by side, send a unit that fails its tests back to the old framework rather than block the rollout or diagnose each failure. Oracle yes; model no; weak. Cases: Uber. Against: none found; a limit from Uber.
- **ROL-9** [stated] Unrequested changes of low priority mostly sit undecided; let owners commit to the generated branch, and consider generating hard-to-check moves only when owners ask. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: Bloomberg. Against: none found.
- **ROL-10** [stated] Shadow agreement on light traffic proves little: aim the old-against-new comparison at the largest and oddest inputs, check each answer is possible at all, and label mismatches by kind. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: GitLab, Temporal. Against: none found; a limit from Temporal.
- **ROL-11** [stated] Cut over in order of how costly a mistake is to undo, often against the direction data flows: read-only paths first, paths whose output leaves the system last, each behind a flag. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: Temporal. Against: none found; a limit from Temporal.

## [Machines and operations](operations.md)

- **OPS-1** [stated] Parallel agents saturate CPU, disk and I/O: size the machine first, let one agent build at a time through a lease, and push full test runs to CI. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun. Against: Asana.
- **OPS-2** [stated] Contain heavy tests with operating-system limits (control groups, process namespaces, disk quotas); asking the agent to be careful contains nothing. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Bun, Lutz Leonhardt. Against: Bun.
- **OPS-3** [stated] Make the inner loop fast (module splits, build caches, host I/O) before scaling agents; their time goes mostly to reading, building and testing, not writing. Oracle no; model partly; strong. Cases: GitHub, Bun, Shopify, Asana, Mindstone. Against: Shopify.
- **OPS-4** [stated] List what the old runtime supplied silently (time zone, environment, process flags) and test every platform you ship; one green platform says little. Oracle yes; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Spotify. Against: none found.
- **OPS-5** [stated] Keep hardening after merge: repeated security review, round-the-clock fuzzing and leak tracking, with people reviewing the fixes they produce. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: Bun. Against: disagree: Bun.
- **OPS-6** [stated] Run bulk change jobs, by agent or by rule, as scheduled batches sized to the infrastructure, sort results into status groups, and rerun only what is stuck. Oracle partly; model no; strong. Cases: Slack, Google, Airbnb, Uber. Against: Bloomberg.
- **OPS-7** [ours] Load-test the new code for blocking and resource exhaustion; one port froze its interface on a synchronous call across the bridge. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub. Against: none found.
- **OPS-8** [stated] Running old and new paths side by side can double the load on shared services such as caches and rate-limit stores; check their headroom first, since raising it may need infrastructure work. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: GitLab. Against: none found.

## [Security](security.md)

- **SEC-1** [stated] Run unattended agents in a minimal sandbox with an allowlist of commands; pushing, merging and talking to people belong to the surrounding infrastructure. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Spotify. Against: Bun, Christopher Chedeau.
- **SEC-2** [stated] Whatever the harness exposes may get used unasked (an unlisted skill, git commands, a peer's worktree); remove what the task does not need. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun, Spotify. Against: disagree: Spotify.
- **SEC-3** [ours] Block destructive repository and system commands in the tool layer, not with a prompt rule, which only arrives after the damage. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Bun, Spotify. Against: none found; a limit from Christopher Chedeau.
- **SEC-4** [stated] After a port into a memory-safe language, count where unsafe code sits, allow it only at foreign and system boundaries, and have the compiler forbid it elsewhere. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun, Intel. Against: disagree: Bun.
- **SEC-5** [stated] Generate foreign-function signatures with a binding tool and reject any model answer that differs; a wrong contract leaks unsafety into safe-looking code. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: Intel. Against: none found.
- **SEC-6** [ours] A bounds-checked target turns silent out-of-range access into crashes; expect new crash reports and test limits at real-world sizes. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: Bun. Against: none found.
- **SEC-7** [ours] Treat each replaced library as a migration of its own, above all sanitizers, credential stores and protocol SDKs, and vet every new dependency. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub. Against: none found.
- **SEC-8** [stated] Treat agent session logs and traces as data that may hold secrets; control where they are stored and where they are uploaded. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Spotify. Against: none found.
- **SEC-9** [stated] Isolate each agent run from earlier attempts and reference answers, which it could otherwise read and lean on; decide about network access too. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Intel, Bloomberg. Against: none found.
- **SEC-10** [stated] Never let agents choose the order of schema changes, backfills or ownership of shared tables; one agent's chosen order would have lost data silently. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: 1Password. Against: none found.

## [Cost](cost.md)

- **CST-1** [stated] Long agent runs are affordable only with high prompt-cache reuse: keep a stable prompt prefix and track the hit rate and each kind of token. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun. Against: Zalando.
- **CST-2** [ours] Ask for the full bill: tokens at the price paid, people's hours by role, compute and CI, review, and the work after merge; most sources give one piece. Oracle no; model no; strong. Cases: GitHub, Bun, Airbnb, Spotify, Ping.gg, PagerDuty. Against: GitHub.
- **CST-3** [ours] Expect cost per unit to have a long tail; report median and mean, and size the budget for hub components and hard files. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Intel, GitHub, Airbnb. Against: none found.
- **CST-4** [ours] Before reusing a published cost, check the model, how it was reached and the price basis; pre-release, internal or partner models give costs others cannot repeat. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, Intel, Google, Asana, Ping.gg. Against: none found.
- **CST-5** [ours] Work out cost per unit inside one case and name the unit; added lines, production lines, symbols and files differ, and tokens do not convert to money across cases. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub, Intel. Against: none found.
- **CST-6** [ours] Count the work after merge (regression fixes, security rounds, fuzzing, clean-up and speed work) in what the migration cost. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub. Against: none found.
- **CST-7** [ours] Budget review agents as a multiple of generation (several reviewers and a fixer per writer), and ask for their share of tokens, which no case reports. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub. Against: none found.
- **CST-8** [stated] Missing or broken tests in target repositories, or checks the pipeline cannot run, shift the cost of checking onto the teams that receive the changes; the central figures leave it out. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: Spotify, Google, Bloomberg. Against: none found.
- **CST-9** [ours] Pipeline and harness costs pay back over many repositories or migrations; a one-off project should reuse a general harness rather than build one. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: Spotify. Against: disagree: Airbnb, Slack.

## [Team and roles](team.md)

- **TEM-1** [stated] The lead engineer's job becomes running the control loop: framing slices, challenging design, pushing for completeness, deciding every merge. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun, Christopher Chedeau, Ladybird. Against: GitHub, PagerDuty.
- **TEM-2** [stated] Count the people behind a one-engineer story (reviewers in many teams, interop, packaging and build specialists) and staff and budget for them. Oracle no; model no; strong. Cases: GitHub, Google, Slack, PagerDuty. Against: Bun, Christopher Chedeau.
- **TEM-3** [stated] A central team should own the agent tooling, build it with early adopters, and teach prompt writing; untrained users fell into the same traps. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Spotify, Slack. Against: none found.
- **TEM-4** [stated] Review in two tiers: the migration owner screens each batch, then code owners accept; expect the load to spread over many teams. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Google, Spotify, Bloomberg. Against: Bun.
- **TEM-5** [stated] Code the model migrates is code the team never wrote; keep owners close to it and teach them the new library, or debugging and incident handling suffer. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: Zalando. Against: Ping.gg, Christopher Chedeau.
- **TEM-6** [stated] Budget for the people: engineers new to agents lose days going in circles, and steering agents that cut corners, then reviewing all they produce, wears people out. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Mindstone, GitLab. Against: none found; a limit from Mindstone, GitLab.

## [Rule-based tools and AI](tooling.md)

- **TOL-1** [stated] Have agents build deterministic tools (analysers, call-site manifests, porting guides, ownership tables), review those, then bind later agent work to them. Oracle no; model partly; strong. Cases: 1Password, Bun, Intel, Christopher Chedeau. Against: 1Password.
- **TOL-2** [stated] Run a rule-based codemod first and give the model its partial output, with a note wherever the rules gave up; it anchors the model. Oracle partly; model yes; medium; may be outdated. Cases: Slack, Google. Against: Uber.
- **TOL-3** [stated] Find change sites with a code index or static analysis, include too many rather than too few, and let the model edit the whole file around each hint. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: Google, 1Password. Against: Google.
- **TOL-4** [stated] Price the rule-based alternative with the upkeep of its rules; hand-written transforms keep growing on long-tail patterns, which is where models pay off. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Spotify, Slack, Google, Zalando. Against: disagree: Uber, Slack.
- **TOL-5** [stated] Keep agents and models behind your own thin interface, log traces from day one, and pin model and settings per run; the best agent changed within a year. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Spotify, Google. Against: disagree: GitHub.
- **TOL-6** [stated] Set up linters, formatters, type checks and coding instructions before the first change, and run them inside the agent's loop, not only in CI. Oracle no; model partly; strong. Cases: GitHub, Spotify, Airbnb, Slack, Temporal. Against: Shopify.
- **TOL-7** [stated] Before choosing a model for a mechanical framework move, try deterministic rewrites on a typed syntax tree; at very large scale they were judged more practical. Oracle partly; model partly; weak. Cases: Uber. Against: Slack, Airbnb.
- **TOL-8** [stated] Give agents a direct way to inspect and drive the running app (state, events, commands, logic run headless); screenshots and accessibility trees made each test take minutes. Oracle partly; model partly; weak. Cases: Shopify. Against: none found; a limit from Shopify.
- **TOL-9** [stated] Where the old format is regular, have the model fill a schema-checked data object and let templates write the new files; one template fix then repairs every target. Oracle partly; model partly; weak. Cases: Bloomberg. Against: none found; a limit from Bloomberg.
- **TOL-10** [stated] At each model upgrade, review the pre-processing built to cover the older model's gaps; keep a step only if it adds reproducibility or eases debugging. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Bloomberg. Against: Bloomberg.

## [Context and prompts](context.md)

- **CTX-1** [stated] Choosing the right context (nearby files, good examples, runtime data, exact mapping tables) moved results more than polishing the prompt wording. Oracle partly; model yes; strong. Cases: Airbnb, Slack, Spotify, Zalando, Asana, Datadog. Against: disagree: Spotify, Zalando, Asana.
- **CTX-2** [stated] Give the model the runtime facts a person would look at, such as the rendered output of each test, not only the source file. Oracle yes; model partly; medium. Cases: Slack, Zalando, Shopify, Bloomberg. Against: none found.
- **CTX-3** [stated] Write field and API mappings out explicitly, such as in tables, and have a person check them against what each side means; a guide adapted from the human one, and mappings by name, went wrong. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Spotify, Zalando. Against: Asana.
- **CTX-4** [stated] State the whole end state, its preconditions and when not to act; agents read vague goals narrowly and leave parts of the work out of scope. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: GitHub, Spotify, 1Password, Zalando, Robert Marshall, Mindstone, GitLab. Against: 1Password.
- **CTX-5** [stated] Put one change in each prompt; prompts bundling several changes ran out of context or stopped halfway. Oracle no; model yes; medium. Cases: Spotify, Zalando, Datadog. Against: Zalando.
- **CTX-6** [stated] Prefer large, static, version-controlled prompts and few tools for predictability; letting the agent fetch context through many tools adds variance. Oracle no; model yes; weak. Cases: Spotify. Against: disagree: Spotify, GitHub, Asana, Zalando.
- **CTX-7** [stated] Ask the agent after each session what its prompt lacked, and fold the answer into the next version of the prompt. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Spotify. Against: none found.
- **CTX-8** [stated] Fit the prompt to the agent: a weak home-built loop needed step-by-step lists, while a stronger agent did better with the end state and room to plan. Oracle no; model yes; weak. Cases: Spotify, Asana. Against: Asana, 1Password.
- **CTX-9** [stated] When the context budget is small, choose context by fixed rules: full bodies of nearby functions, signatures for the rest, the hardest callers first. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: Intel. Against: Airbnb.
- **CTX-10** [stated] Agents learn from the repository as it stands: fix docs and agent guidance that still favour or point at the old code, and awkward examples, or they spread. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Asana, Temporal. Against: none found; a limit from Temporal.
- **CTX-11** [stated] Keep each unit small enough for the agent to read whole, such as one function per file in the target; very long files were refused or read in loose chunks and filled the context. Oracle no; model yes; weak. Cases: Christopher Chedeau. Against: none found.
- **CTX-12** [stated] Before porting, have a model write down why each old function exists and what behaviour it protects, and give those notes with every prompt; they cut the rounds per unit. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Datadog. Against: none found; a limit from Datadog.
- **CTX-13** [stated] Keep a rule for agents in an instruction file beside the code it governs, not at the root, and name the test enforcing it, so a reader can tell when the rule has expired. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Temporal. Against: none found; a limit from Temporal.

## [Many agents at once](orchestration.md)

- **ORC-1** [stated] Agents sharing one working copy wreck each other's work; give each writer its own worktree, or restrict git to committing its own files. Oracle no; model partly; strong. Cases: Bun, 1Password, GitHub, Shopify, Lutz Leonhardt. Against: Bun, Lutz Leonhardt.
- **ORC-2** [stated] Run agents in parallel only on changes that are independent by design; otherwise parallelism adds inconsistency. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: 1Password, Asana, Bun. Against: Bun.
- **ORC-3** [stated] Peer agents on adjacent code need a named coordinator or human tiebreaker, and autonomy must stop at anything outside the agent's own branch. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: GitHub. Against: GitHub.
- **ORC-4** [stated] Build the work queue from deterministic output (compiler errors by module, failing traces per command), run the tool once, then fan the items out. Oracle partly; model no; strong. Cases: Bun, Airbnb. Against: disagree: GitHub, Bun.
- **ORC-5** [stated] Within one workspace, fan reading out to subagents and keep the edits with one agent; reading far outnumbered editing. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: GitHub. Against: GitHub, Bun.
- **ORC-6** [stated] Prefer a short leash to a complex multi-agent design where you can: fixed code picks context, order and output place, and the model translates one unit. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: Intel, Bloomberg. Against: disagree: Bun, GitHub, Shopify, Asana.

## [Agent failure modes](agent-failures.md)

- **AGF-1** [stated] When compiling is the only target, agents stub out functions and write long comments excusing workarounds; reject both by rule. Oracle no; model yes; medium. Cases: Bun, Intel, Christopher Chedeau. Against: Intel, Christopher Chedeau.
- **AGF-2** [stated] Agents fill gaps in the spec with plausible guesses and carry them through many edits; make them check formats and ownership against code or data, or stop and ask. Oracle no; model yes; strong. Cases: 1Password, GitHub, Spotify, Zalando. Against: 1Password.
- **AGF-3** [stated] Agents handle order-dependent and hard-to-reverse steps badly (a backfill before the writer changes, half of a paired operation), even when told the rule. Oracle partly; model yes; medium. Cases: 1Password, GitHub. Against: none found.
- **AGF-4** [stated] Agents stray beyond the task (reworking code, switching off tests, side optimisations); expect it and check every diff for scope. Oracle no; model yes; medium. Cases: Spotify, GitHub, Google, Zalando. Against: GitHub.
- **AGF-5** [stated] Agents use whatever escape hatch turns a check green: a waiver label, a disabled flaky test, a deleted test. Oracle partly; model yes; medium. Cases: GitHub, Spotify, Christopher Chedeau, Mindstone. Against: none found.
- **AGF-6** [ours] Make each agent session discardable as a unit; one unchecked assumption forced a whole session to be rolled back. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: 1Password, Christopher Chedeau, Lutz Leonhardt, Robert Marshall. Against: none found; a limit from Lutz Leonhardt.
- **AGF-7** [stated] Output varies between runs on the same input: plan retries, pick among passing attempts, and contain the variance in production migrations. Oracle partly; model yes; medium. Cases: Google, 1Password, Spotify, Zalando, Bloomberg. Against: none found.
- **AGF-8** [stated] Check how well the model handles each language in scope; one poorly supported language fell back to people. Oracle no; model yes; weak; may be outdated. Cases: Google. Against: none found.
- **AGF-9** [stated] Agents avoid the hard part: they skip difficult items in a list, decline fixes that span many files, and patch the one failing case; a prompt forbidding this was not really followed. Oracle no; model yes; weak. Cases: Christopher Chedeau, PagerDuty, Mindstone. Against: none found; a limit from Christopher Chedeau.

## [Human oversight](oversight.md)

- **OVS-1** [stated] The agent that changes the code must not change what counts as correct: edits to tests, snapshots, baselines and waiver labels need a separate owner's approval. Oracle partly; model partly; medium. Cases: GitHub, Spotify, Bun, Intel, Christopher Chedeau. Against: disagree: Mindstone, Ladybird.
- **OVS-2** [stated] Keep the final merge with a person who checks how the agent answered CI and review, not only the diff. Oracle no; model partly; strong. Cases: GitHub, Google, Slack. Against: disagree: Bun, Ping.gg.
- **OVS-3** [stated] Decide up front where automation stops (a retry cap, a residue size, a category for people) and hand over with the failed attempt as the starting point. Oracle no; model no; strong. Cases: Airbnb, 1Password, Google, Bloomberg, GitLab. Against: Uber.
- **OVS-4** [stated] Bind each human approval to the exact text approved, such as a hash of the plan, so any later edit to the plan needs a fresh approval. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: Shopify. Against: none found.
- **OVS-5** [stated] Run agents in small waves that mix simple targets with known edge cases, and make the orchestrator stop for a person's approval between them, so one systematic mistake cannot spread to every target. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Lutz Leonhardt. Against: none found; a limit from Lutz Leonhardt.

## [Knowledge capture](knowledge.md)

- **KNW-1** [stated] When a failure recurs, fix what generates the code (prompt, reviewer rule, skill, evaluation, harness), not only the output; the second time is the trigger. Oracle no; model no; strong. Cases: Bun, GitHub, Airbnb, Uber, Zalando, Shopify, Bloomberg, Christopher Chedeau, PagerDuty, Mindstone, Checkly. Against: Christopher Chedeau, 1Password.
- **KNW-2** [stated] Stamp each unit with its status, tune against the largest failing group using a small sample, then sweep all units again. Oracle partly; model no; strong. Cases: Airbnb, Slack, Google, Uber. Against: none found.
- **KNW-3** [stated] Keep structured session logs from the start; they later answered where time went and what people did, and became evaluations. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub. Against: GitHub.
- **KNW-4** [stated] A compacted or fresh session forgets what the last one learned; keep the method in files it rereads (instructions, one debug script) and find work by search, not a growing notes file. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Christopher Chedeau, Datadog. Against: disagree: PagerDuty, Christopher Chedeau, Temporal.
- **KNW-5** [stated] Mark temporary migration code the day you write it with what it is for and how to remove it; an agent can later find the notes and work through them as the removal list. Oracle no; model partly; weak. Cases: Temporal. Against: none found; a limit from Temporal.

## [Measuring and reading results](measurement.md)

- **MSR-1** [ours] Treat savings measured against a manual effort that never ran as self-estimates; record the basis beside each figure and never add them across cases. Oracle no; model no; strong. Cases: Google, Spotify, Airbnb, Slack, Bun, 1Password, PagerDuty, Mindstone. Against: Google.
- **MSR-2** [ours] For every success rate ask out of what (attempted, opened, merged, dropped from scope), and report each measure with its base; bases differed several-fold. Oracle no; model no; strong. Cases: Spotify, Slack, Zalando, Bloomberg, Lutz Leonhardt. Against: Airbnb.
- **MSR-3** [ours] Weigh each source by the author's stake in the tool (seller, owner, partner); none of the cases had outside measurement. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, GitHub, Spotify, 1Password, Intel. Against: Google, Slack.
- **MSR-4** [stated] Credit a gain to the migration only after separating it from work that landed in the same window (other speed work, linker changes, unrelated fixes). Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun. Against: disagree: Bun.
- **MSR-5** [stated] Escaped defects are unknown by nature: publish known regressions as a floor, grouped by cause, and use a before-and-after proxy labelled as a proxy. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: GitHub, Bun. Against: Airbnb.
- **MSR-6** [ours] Activity numbers (lines per minute, commits, merged changes) are not progress; track verified behaviour or the shrinking list of remaining sites. Oracle partly; model no; medium. Cases: Bun, Spotify, GitHub, Christopher Chedeau, Ping.gg. Against: none found.
- **MSR-7** [ours] Re-date a lesson before reusing it: early negative results, and results from pre-release or restricted models, may not hold for the models you use. Oracle no; model partly; medium. Cases: Slack, Bun, Intel, Google, Uber. Against: 1Password.
- **MSR-8** [ours] Do not credit the model with work the deterministic tools did: finding sites, building manifests and codemods were often the hard part. Oracle no; model no; strong. Cases: Google, Slack, 1Password, Spotify, Uber, Bloomberg. Against: Bun.
- **MSR-9** [stated] If you will claim savings, measure people's share from file snapshots or logs from day one; estimates from the tool's own builders are biased. Oracle no; model no; medium. Cases: Google, Temporal. Against: Google.
- **MSR-10** [stated] A merge rate undercounts unrequested changes: also count targets whose owners rejected the change and then migrated anyway, often reusing it. Oracle no; model no; weak. Cases: Bloomberg. Against: none found; a limit from Bloomberg.
